items.stem: Addams's account suggests that the striking girls' vulnerability came mainly from
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

"At a meeting of working girls held at Hull House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened were those who had no one to stand by them..."
—Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull House, 1910 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: The passage says nothing about the strikers' education — their fear came from economic dependence, not from being uneducated. Education is never mentioned as the source of vulnerability.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Addams stresses that the strikers 'paying board' were 'most easily frightened' — fear of eviction from their boardinghouses broke strikes. Their vulnerability came from depending on employers and landlords for housing.
option_explanations.C: Federal strikebreaking injunctions were a real Gilded Age weapon, but Addams's account does not mention them — the fear she describes comes from housing dependence, not court orders.
option_explanations.D: The passage never mentions immigration status — the vulnerability described is economic (fear of eviction), not about how recently anyone arrived.

items.stem: Hull House's role in the shoe-factory strike illustrates settlement houses' function as
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

"At a meeting of working girls held at Hull House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened were those who had no one to stand by them..."
—Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull House, 1910 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. The strike meeting happened at Hull House itself — settlement houses served as meeting places where workers could gather and organize. They were not job agencies, missions, or government offices.
option_explanations.B: Hull House was not a job-placement agency — it did not find factory jobs for workers. Its function here was providing organizing space, not employment services.
option_explanations.C: Hull House was not a religious mission — Addams's settlement was secular and social, not evangelical. It did not seek to convert immigrants.
option_explanations.D: Hull House was not a government relief office — it was a private settlement house. Its role was as a neighborhood institution supporting workers, not as a state agency.

items.explanation: 'A boarding club of our own' so workers could 'stand behind each other' is mutual aid — the cooperative impulse behind Progressive Era labor reform. Scientific management, nativism, and laissez-faire point the opposite way.
options: A. Scientific management of factories
B. Nativist Americanization programs
C. Laissez-faire individualism
D. Working-class mutual aid and cooperation
items.stem: The strikers' proposal for a 'boarding club of our own' most directly reflects which Progressive Era idea?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

"At a meeting of working girls held at Hull House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened were those who had no one to stand by them..."
—Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull House, 1910 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Scientific management (Taylorism) was about factory efficiency and timed work — the opposite of workers cooperating to protect each other. It points away from mutual aid.
option_explanations.B: Nativist Americanization programs sought to assimilate immigrants to American norms — a top-down, often coercive project, not workers building their own cooperative institutions.
option_explanations.C: Laissez-faire individualism is the opposite of the boarding club idea — the club is collective self-help, not every-worker-for-herself.
option_explanations.D: Correct. 'A boarding club of our own' so workers could 'stand behind each other' is working-class mutual aid and cooperation — the cooperative impulse behind Progressive Era labor reform.

options: A. Giving direct cash payments to striking workers

C. Settling in the neighborhood and supporting workers' own organizations

items.stem: Addams's approach at Hull House differed from earlier charity models by
items.stimulus:

option_explanations.A: Hull House did not give direct cash payments to strikers — Addams's approach was to support workers' own organizations, not to pay them. Cash relief was the old charity model.
option_explanations.B: Hull House did not lobby Congress for open immigration — its work was local and social, not a federal immigration campaign. Immigration restriction politics came later.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Settlement differed from older charity by residence: reformers lived in the ward and enabled workers' own organizations rather than dispensing alms from a distance. Hull House never paid strikers or ran candidates.
option_explanations.D: Hull House did not run settlement workers for political office — its model was neighborhood residence and organizing support, not electoral politics.

items.stem: After the Revolution, many Founders believed
items.stimulus:

option_explanations.A: Correct. Many Founders — Jefferson included — expected slavery to gradually wither away, a hope the cotton gin and westward expansion would destroy.
option_explanations.B: Founders did not believe freeing slaves should be outlawed — several (Jefferson, Washington in his will) freed or planned to free enslaved people. Outlawing manumission was never their view.
option_explanations.C: Founders did not believe slavery would anchor the economy — many thought it was economically backwards and morally embarrassing, expecting its decline.

items.explanation: The Constitution's slavery compromise barred Congress from banning slave importation for twenty years — until 1808 — without ever naming slavery.

items.stem: Which was a reference to slavery in the Constitution?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[A colonial-era advertisement announcing the sale of newly imported enslaved Africans at Charleston, listing their numbers and terms of sale.]

option_explanations.A: The Northwest Ordinance (1787) was a separate act of the Confederation Congress, not part of the Constitution. The Constitution's own slavery references were the three-fifths clause, the fugitive slave clause, and the importation clause.
option_explanations.B: The Constitution never outlawed slavery above the Mason-Dixon Line — that was the Missouri Compromise's line (1820), decades later. The Constitution protected slavery where it existed.
option_explanations.C: The Constitution did not say slavery could never be outlawed — it allowed Congress to ban slave importation after 1808 and said nothing barring future abolition. 'Never' overstates the compromise.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Constitution's slavery compromise barred Congress from banning slave importation for twenty years — until 1808 — without ever using the word 'slavery.'

President Kennedy declared that just as earlier generations had ridden the first waves of industrial revolution and invention, his generation must conquer the new frontiers of science and space.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Kennedy's frontier was metaphorical — 'the new frontiers of science and space' plus unmet domestic needs — not literal western territory.

option_explanations.C: The Iron Curtain was a Cold War reality Kennedy addressed, but it was never his 'frontier' metaphor — the frontier was about science, space, and domestic problems.
option_explanations.D: Ocean depths and polar regions were never Kennedy's frontier metaphor — his New Frontier was science, space, and unmet social needs.

items.stimulus:

option_explanations.C: Isolationist withdrawal was the opposite of the platform — it called for renewed American leadership abroad, not retreat.
option_explanations.D: Rolling back New Deal programs was the opposite of the platform — it called for expanding the federal role, not dismantling it.

items.stem: Logan's speech best illustrates which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following excerpt.

"I appeal to any white man to say if ever he entered Logan's cabin hungry and he gave him not meat... During the course of the last long and bloody war Logan remained idle in his cabin, an advocate for peace... I had even thought to have lived with you but for the injuries of one man. Colonel Cresap, the last spring, in cold blood and unprovoked, murdered all the relations of Logan... There runs not a drop of my blood in the veins of any living creature. This called on me for revenge. I have sought it. I have killed many... But do not harbor a thought that mine is the joy of fear. Logan never felt fear."
—Logan (Tah-gah-jute), speech recorded 1774 (abridged)
options: A. Native leaders uniformly rejected all diplomacy and negotiation with colonists
B. British officials successfully mediated frontier disputes between settlers and tribes
C. Cycles of personal revenge and retaliatory violence shaped frontier relations
D. The Proclamation of 1763 permanently ended all frontier violence
items.explanation: Logan describes a personal cycle: his friendship with whites, Cresap's murder of his family, and his revenge killings — illustrating how frontier violence escalated through retaliation.

option_explanations.A: Logan's speech does not show Native leaders uniformly rejecting diplomacy — Logan himself describes having been 'an advocate for peace' before his family was murdered. The speech is about revenge, not a blanket rejection of negotiation.
option_explanations.B: British officials did not successfully mediate this dispute — the speech describes unmediated cycles of killing. No successful British mediation appears in Logan's account.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Logan describes a personal cycle: his friendship with whites, Cresap's murder of his family, and his own revenge killings — illustrating how frontier violence escalated through personal revenge and retaliation.
option_explanations.D: The Proclamation of 1763 did not end frontier violence — Logan's 1774 speech describes violence continuing a decade later. The Proclamation was widely ignored by settlers.

items.explanation: Long proposed liquidating large personal fortunes through steep wealth, income, and inheritance taxes to fund direct payments to the less well-off.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Long proposed liquidating large personal fortunes through steep wealth, income, and inheritance taxes to fund homesteads, guaranteed incomes, and pensions for the less well-off.
option_explanations.B: Long did not propose a balanced budget — his plan required massive new spending funded by taxing the rich. Fiscal balance was never his mechanism.
option_explanations.C: Long did not propose foreign loans — his funding came from taxing American fortunes, not borrowing from European creditors.
option_explanations.D: Long did not propose returning to the gold standard — his plan was about redistribution through taxation, not monetary policy.

items.stem: Long's assassination in 1935
items.stimulus:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following excerpt.

Senator Huey Long charged that a tiny elite hoarded the nation's wealth while millions suffered in the Depression. He proposed capping personal fortunes, guaranteeing every family a homestead and a minimum annual income, shortening the workweek, and providing free college and old-age pensions — all funded by steep taxes on the rich.
—After Huey P. Long, 'Share Our Wealth' radio address, February 1934 (paraphrased)
options: A. Removed the leading left-populist challenger to the New Deal
B. Led to Long's election as president in 1936
C. Caused the Supreme Court to strike down the NRA as unconstitutional
D. Triggered American entry into World War II
items.explanation: Long was shot at the Louisiana state capitol in September 1935; his death removed the leading left-populist rival who had been pressuring Roosevelt.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Long was shot at the Louisiana state capitol in September 1935; his death removed the leading left-populist challenger who had been pressuring Roosevelt.
option_explanations.B: Long was assassinated in 1935 — he could not be elected president in 1936. Death ended his candidacy, it did not create one.
option_explanations.C: The Supreme Court struck down the NRA in Schechter (1935) on its own legal grounds — Long's assassination had nothing to do with it.
option_explanations.D: Long's assassination did not trigger American entry into World War II — the U.S. entered in December 1941, six years later, after Pearl Harbor.

items.stem: Bradford's account of Squanto illustrates
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)
options: A. The complete absence of Native-colonist contact
B. The total military dominance of the Pilgrims
C. The critical role of Native aid in colonial survival
D. Spanish missionary influence in New England
items.explanation: Bradford credits Squanto with teaching the Pilgrims to plant corn, fish, and navigate — aid without which the colony might not have survived.

option_explanations.A: The passage shows extensive Native-colonist contact — Squanto lived with the Pilgrims and guided them. 'Complete absence of contact' contradicts the entire account.
option_explanations.B: The passage shows no Pilgrim military dominance — the Pilgrims were weak and dependent, saved by Squanto's help. Military dominance is the opposite of the story.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bradford credits Squanto with teaching the Pilgrims to plant corn, fish, and navigate — aid without which the colony might not have survived. The account illustrates how critical Native help was.
option_explanations.D: There was no Spanish missionary influence in New England — the Spanish never operated in Plymouth. The aid came from the Wampanoags, not Spanish missions.

items.stem: Bradford's description of Squanto as 'a special instrument sent of God' reflects
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)
options: A. Enlightenment rationalism and confidence in human reason
B. Deist philosophy and a distant, nonintervening God
C. Puritan providentialism — the belief that God directed events
D. Anglican ritualism and sacramental worship
items.explanation: Bradford interprets Squanto's aid as divine providence — the Puritan habit of reading God's hand in historical events.

option_explanations.A: Enlightenment rationalism belonged to the 18th century — Bradford wrote in the 17th century, and 'instrument sent of God' is providential, not rationalist.
option_explanations.B: Deism's distant, nonintervening God is the opposite of Bradford's view — he sees God actively sending Squanto. Providence, not deism, is his framework.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bradford interprets Squanto's aid as divine providence — the Puritan habit of reading God's directing hand in historical events.
option_explanations.D: Anglican ritualism and sacramental worship were what the Puritans rejected — Bradford was a Separatist, not an Anglican. The passage reflects Puritan providentialism.

items.stem: The Pilgrims' survival at Plymouth depended most directly on
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)
options: A. Discoveries of gold and other mineral wealth nearby
B. The fur trade conducted with the Dutch
C. Wampanoag aid and adaptation to new agricultural conditions
D. Tobacco cultivation for export to England
items.explanation: Squanto and the Wampanoags taught the Pilgrims corn planting and fishing — the agricultural knowledge that made survival possible.

option_explanations.A: The Pilgrims found no gold or mineral wealth — New England had none. Mineral wealth was a Spanish and southern story, not Plymouth's.
option_explanations.B: The fur trade with the Dutch came later and was not what kept the Pilgrims alive in the first years — survival depended on learning to grow food.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Squanto and the Wampanoags taught the Pilgrims corn planting and fishing — the agricultural knowledge and adaptation to new conditions that made survival possible.
option_explanations.D: Tobacco was Virginia's crop, not Plymouth's — the Pilgrims did not grow tobacco for export. Their survival came from corn and fish, learned from the Wampanoags.

items.stem: Bradford's history is best characterized as
items.stimulus:
Questions 45–48 refer to the following excerpt.

"Squanto... was a special instrument sent of God for their good beyond their expectation. He directed them how to set their corn, where to take fish, and to procure other commodities, and was also their pilot to bring them to unknown places for their profit, and never left them till he died."
—William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation (abridged)
options: A. A Loyalist polemic against the Revolution
B. A Federalist essay on constitutional government
C. A transcendentalist meditation on nature
D. A firsthand Puritan chronicle of history and providence
items.explanation: Of Plymouth Plantation is the classic Puritan primary source — an eyewitness history that constantly interprets events as God's providence.

option_explanations.A: Bradford's history is not a Loyalist polemic — he wrote in the 1600s, a century before the Revolution. Loyalism did not exist in his time.
option_explanations.B: Bradford's history is not a Federalist essay — the Federalists belonged to the 1780s–90s. Bradford wrote a century and a half earlier.
option_explanations.C: Bradford's history is not transcendentalist — transcendentalism was an 1840s movement. Bradford's work is 17th-century Puritan chronicle.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Of Plymouth Plantation is the classic Puritan primary source — an eyewitness history that constantly interprets events as God's providence.

items.stem: The poster's imagery was designed primarily to
items.stimulus:

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']
options: A. Document actual frontier life with strict accuracy
B. Romanticize the West for eastern and European audiences

items.explanation: The Wild West show was entertainment that packaged a romanticized frontier — cowboys, 'Indians,' sharpshooters — for paying audiences in the East and Europe.

option_explanations.A: The poster was advertising, not documentation — the Wild West show was staged entertainment, not a factual record of frontier life.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Wild West show was entertainment that packaged a romanticized frontier — cowboys, 'Indians,' sharpshooters — for paying audiences in the East and Europe.
option_explanations.C: The poster did not recruit soldiers — the Indian Wars were largely over by the 1890s, and the show was commercial entertainment, not a military recruiting tool.
option_explanations.D: The poster did not promote railroad bonds — it advertised Buffalo Bill's show. Railroad investment was a different enterprise entirely.

items.stem: The Wild West show's portrayal of Native Americans

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']

items.explanation: The shows staged 'Indian attacks' and battle reenactments that fixed stereotypes of Native Americans as savage foes in the popular imagination.

option_explanations.A: The show did not accurately represent tribal cultures — its 'Indian attacks' were staged spectacles, not ethnography.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The shows staged 'Indian attacks' and battle reenactments that fixed stereotypes of Native Americans as savage foes in the popular imagination.
option_explanations.C: The show did not oppose federal Indian policy — it entertained within the reservation era's assumptions, not against them.
option_explanations.D: The show did not end the reservation system — it was entertainment, and the reservation system continued for decades.

items.stem: The popularity of such shows in the 1890s reflected

option_explanations.B: The shows' popularity did not reflect the Populist Party's rise — the Populists were a farm protest movement, unconnected to Wild West entertainment.
option_explanations.C: Correct. As the census declared the frontier closed (1890) and America industrialized, eastern audiences romanticized a West that was already disappearing — nostalgia for a 'vanishing' frontier.
option_explanations.D: The Alaska gold discovery (1896–98) was a separate event — the shows' popularity reflected frontier nostalgia, not gold-rush news.

items.stem: A historian using this poster as evidence would most appropriately use it to study

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']

option_explanations.B: The poster is not evidence of treaty terms — it advertises a show, not diplomacy. Treaty terms come from documents, not posters.
option_explanations.C: The poster is not evidence of cowboys' actual wages — it shows a staged spectacle, not payroll records.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The poster is evidence of popular culture and western mythmaking — how commercial entertainment constructed the romantic West — not of frontier realities.

items.stem: Bush's 'new world order' rhetoric was prompted most directly by
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following excerpt.

In a September 1990 address to Congress, President Bush argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait offered a chance to build 'a new world order' — in which nations would cooperate through the United Nations to deter aggression, pursue shared prosperity, and uphold the rule of law, with America leading a collective-security effort.
—After President George H. W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, September 1990 (paraphrased)
options: A. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990
B. The fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989
C. The Iranian Revolution of 1979
D. The Vietnam War and its aftermath
items.explanation: Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait triggered the crisis Bush answered with his 'new world order' vision of collective security.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Iraq's August 1990 invasion of Kuwait triggered the crisis Bush answered with his 'new world order' vision of collective security through the United Nations.
option_explanations.B: The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989 — it shaped the post–Cold War context but did not prompt the 'new world order' speech, which was about Kuwait.
option_explanations.C: The Iranian Revolution belonged to 1979 — a decade earlier. It was not the prompt for Bush's 1990 address.
option_explanations.D: Vietnam ended in 1975 — fifteen years before the speech. The prompt was Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, not Vietnam's aftermath.

items.stem: The vision Bush described drew most directly on the tradition of
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following excerpt.

In a September 1990 address to Congress, President Bush argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait offered a chance to build 'a new world order' — in which nations would cooperate through the United Nations to deter aggression, pursue shared prosperity, and uphold the rule of law, with America leading a collective-security effort.
—After President George H. W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, September 1990 (paraphrased)
options: A. Wilsonian internationalism and collective security
B. Isolationism and avoidance of foreign entanglements

items.explanation: Bush's call for nations to act together through the UN against aggression echoes Wilson's collective-security ideal from the League of Nations era.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Bush's call for nations to act together through the UN against aggression echoes Wilson's collective-security ideal from the League of Nations era.
option_explanations.B: Isolationism was the opposite of Bush's vision — he called for American-led international cooperation, not avoidance of entanglements.
option_explanations.C: The Monroe Doctrine focused on the Western Hemisphere — Bush's vision was global collective security, not hemispheric doctrine.
option_explanations.D: Nixon's détente was about managing rivalry with the Soviets — Bush's vision was about collective security against aggression, a Wilsonian rather than Nixonian tradition.

items.stem: The Gulf War that followed demonstrated
items.stimulus:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following excerpt.

In a September 1990 address to Congress, President Bush argued that Iraq's invasion of Kuwait offered a chance to build 'a new world order' — in which nations would cooperate through the United Nations to deter aggression, pursue shared prosperity, and uphold the rule of law, with America leading a collective-security effort.
—After President George H. W. Bush, address to a joint session of Congress, September 1990 (paraphrased)
options: A. The effectiveness of a US-led multinational coalition
B. Soviet opposition to the coalition's military action
C. Congressional refusal to authorize the use of military force
D. The irrelevance of the United Nations in the crisis
items.explanation: The 34-nation coalition's swift expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait (Operation Desert Storm, 1991) seemed to vindicate Bush's collective-security vision.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 34-nation coalition's swift expulsion of Iraqi forces from Kuwait (Operation Desert Storm, 1991) seemed to vindicate Bush's collective-security vision.
option_explanations.B: The Soviet Union did not oppose the coalition — Moscow cooperated with the UN resolutions. Soviet opposition was the opposite of what happened.
option_explanations.C: Congress did authorize military force — it passed the authorization in January 1991. Refusal was the opposite of what happened.
option_explanations.D: The UN was not irrelevant — the coalition acted under UN resolutions. The war seemed to prove the UN's relevance, not its irrelevance.
